articles.title: Can America’s government afford “affordability”?
articles.author: The Economist
articles.body_markdown:
ONE UNSEXY word became the Democrats’ winning battle cry in America’s midterm elections in early November: “affordability”. Donald Trump has not got the message. On November 25th, as fresh data showed annual inflation climbing to 3.8%, his administration proposed another round of tariffs on imports from 14 trading partners. China was threatened with duties of up to 20%, on top of existing levies; Vietnam with as much as 35%. A tax on imports is a peculiar answer to voters’ complaints about living costs.

Democrats have a different answer to America’s affordability woes: open the public purse. Fresh from their midterm triumph, they are promising tax relief, more generous benefits and a helping hand with seemingly every household expense. Yet lavishing more public money on an already booming economy is a peculiar answer, too. GDP surged at a blistering annualised rate of 4.3% in the third quarter, the fastest in three years. Uncle Sam, meanwhile, ran a deficit of 6.2% of GDP last fiscal year, the sort of shortfall usually associated with wars and recessions. Just how much can America afford to spend on making life more affordable?

For starters, America’s affordability crisis hardly looks like an emergency. Affordability comes down to purchasing power, which can be boosted by raising real incomes or bringing down prices. When it comes to earnings, Americans are already doing rather well. Real disposable income per person has risen by 13% since the end of 2019. Real median household income reached a record last year. Grocery prices, the cause of much groaning, rose by less than 2% in the year to September. Even petrol is not that dear by historical standards, once you adjust for inflation.

Joe Biden tried to escape a similar political bind when prices and wages both rose after the pandemic by saying, “Look at this chart”, recalls Bharat Ramamurti, who served as an economic adviser to the former president. “It failed spectacularly.” His fellow Democrats are therefore trying to show voters they are listening, and leaving the chart-making to The Economist.

Hakeem Jeffries, the incoming speaker of the House, has laid out a 100-day agenda to unpick some of Mr Trump’s most unpopular handiwork: restoring tax credits that lower health-insurance premiums; reversing cuts to food stamps and Medicaid, the health-care scheme for the poor; and taking aim at tariffs. All would ease the pressure on households. None amounts to an affordability revolution.

Enter Democrats’ grander plans. Some want to expand tax credits for families with children and subsidise child care, others to let younger Americans enroll in Medicare, the public health programme for the old. Price controls are in vogue, including a cap on credit-card interest rates. Mr Trump could veto it all—or not, if he displays the same willingness to work with Democrats as in his first term (or is swayed by anything with his name on it).

The problem is that affordability is not cheap (see chart 1). Reversing Mr Trump’s cuts to Medicaid and food stamps, restoring health-insurance subsidies and ending his tariff extravaganza—which helped bring in $173bn (0.5% of GDP) in customs duties last fiscal year—would add more than $4trn to deficits over the next decade if enacted without offsets, reckons the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget, a non-partisan bean-counter. Include the extra interest payments and the bill rises to nearly $5trn, roughly as much as Mr Trump’s giant spending bill from last year is projected to add to the debt.

And that is just the beginning. A proposal by Cory Booker, a Democratic senator, to expand the child tax credit could cost $1.4trn over a decade. Universal child-care subsidies could add $750bn. Lowering Medicare’s eligibility age from 65 to 62 may cost hundreds of billions more.

Democrats are out of the White House, so they can afford to dream. But if those dreams are ever paid for with borrowed money, they could turn into an affordability nightmare. America’s fiscal strain is already pushing up borrowing costs. The “term premium”—the extra return investors demand for lending for longer periods—has risen to around one percentage point, according to a Federal Reserve model. Higher long-term yields, in turn, feed through to mortgages. Yale University’s Budget Lab estimates that deficit-raising legislation since 2015 has added $2,500 a year to payments on a typical new mortgage. This helps explain consumers’ persistent gloom. In 2024 Marijn Bolhuis of the IMF and co-authors found that accounting for borrowing costs explained almost three-quarters of the gap between consumer sentiment and what inflation and unemployment predicted in 2023.

Further borrowing may make matters worse. Research from the Dallas Fed suggests that adding ten percentage points to America’s debt-to-GDP ratio could lift long-term Treasury yields by around 0.3 percentage points, based on historical relationships. With deficits already so large, investors may prove even less forgiving. “You could have made a case for not being worried about the Treasury market four or five years ago,” says Ben Harris, a former Treasury chief economist now at the Brookings Institution, a think-tank. “It’s much harder to make that case today.”

The government could spend more while maintaining fiscal prudence by raising taxes. The easiest way to do this is to reverse tax cuts for the wealthy preserved by Mr Trump’s big spending bill. Restoring the top income-tax rate to 39.6%, from 37%, could raise around $420bn over a decade. A rise in the corporate-tax rate from 21% to 26.5%, as Democrats proposed in 2021, plus higher taxes on investment income and large inheritances, could bring the total to nearly $2trn, according to the Yale Budget Lab (see chart 2). That would barely replace the revenue lost from repealing Mr Trump’s ever-expanding tariffs. More ambitious measures, such as scrapping the “qualified business income deduction”, a tax break for business owners, and taxing unrealised capital gains at death, could lift the total to $3.1trn.

Mr Trump and Republicans, reluctant to undo their signature legislative achievement, would bridle at such ideas. More exotic proposals are either peanuts or just nuts. Taxing artificial-intelligence data centres may garner bipartisan support, but a plan by Mark Warner, a Democratic senator, to strip them of generous depreciation allowances would raise merely $30bn over a decade, according to the Tax Foundation, a think-tank. A wealth tax of the sort championed by Elizabeth Warren, a left-wing senator, may bring in far more, but would be a nightmare to administer, easy to dodge and damaging to investment. It would also struggle to win over moderate Democrats, let alone Republicans. Even deeply Democratic California just roundly rejected a billionaire tax.

The Californian experience points to Democrats’ political problem. In America, raising taxes has become poison. Nearly six in ten Americans told a recent Gallup poll that their taxes were too high. Although they are taxed far less than Europeans, Americans pay much more for things like health care and child care. That leaves little spare cash—and no appetite to pay more in tax.

Once the party of higher taxes, Democrats are losing their appetite for deficit reduction. Even though Mr Biden’s Inflation Reduction Act was designed to pay for itself, that vast stimulus package added nearly $2trn to the deficit. Republicans, meanwhile, have repeatedly blown holes in the budget with unfunded tax cuts. Why should Democrats raise taxes to shrink deficits, the argument goes, if Republicans will use the fiscal room to slash tax rates? James Talarico, the incoming senator from Texas, campaigned on a “cost-of-living tax cut for the middle class”.

Faced with an arithmetic problem as stubborn as the donkey that is their party’s spirit animal, Democrats may instead opt for the lowest-hanging barley. A “Medicare for missiles” bargain, for instance, would offer social spending for them, more military spending for Republicans—and little new revenue to pay for either. This may offer Americans some short-term relief at the cost of long-term pain from higher inflation and rising borrowing costs.

Ultimately, soothing cost-of-living grievances requires more than opening the public purse. It means tackling the bottlenecks driving up the cost of housing, health care, child care and energy with looser zoning rules, faster permitting for energy projects, more competition among hospitals and the like. And if Democrats genuinely want a European-style welfare state in which citizens need not cough up for basic services, it is their job to persuade Americans that this deserves handing over a little more dosh to the government.

articles.title: The Gulf survived a short, hot war. A long, cold one will be harder
articles.author: The Economist
articles.body_markdown:
FOR HALF a century trouble elsewhere was often good for business in the Gulf. The Arab-Israeli war of 1973 and subsequent oil embargo sparked an economic boom in the region. Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022 brought an influx of foreign capital and a spike in oil prices. This year trouble came to the Gulf itself. Yet in some ways life is returning to normal—as if the trouble were elsewhere entirely.

Flights and hotels are busier. Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates (UAE), will host a Formula One race and a finance summit in December. In October nine people bought homes in Dubai valued at more than 50m dirhams ($14m), even as Donald Trump threatened to resume a war against Iran that could bring retaliatory missiles and drones raining down on the city once again.

America’s president has retreated from those threats, for now. But danger and disruption remain. In both Washington and the Gulf, many officials expect the conflict to continue throughout 2027, and perhaps until Mr Trump leaves office in January 2029. The Gulf states managed to weather a short, hot war earlier this year. A long, cold one could prove more challenging.

The immediate priority is to keep it cold. None of the six members of the Gulf Co-operation Council (GCC)—Bahrain, Kuwait, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the UAE—wants Mr Trump to make good on his threats of renewed fighting. “Everyone makes their pitch differently, but everyone starts it with ‘please don’t’,” says a Gulf diplomat in Washington.

But they cannot agree on much else. Qatar is desperate to broker a deal between America and Iran in order to get its liquefied natural gas flowing again. Saudi Arabia and the UAE fear it will be another lopsided agreement that empowers Iran. Instead they are urging America to continue strangling Iran’s economy.

If the status quo prevails, the next two years could look much like the past two months. The Strait of Hormuz would be neither fully open nor shut and uncertainty would linger over the Gulf. Claudio Galimberti, the chief economist for Rystad Energy, a consultancy, expects a “fragile pseudo-normalisation” of the strait next year, in which America and Iran gradually relax their blockades. Others think America will maintain both its blockade of Iranian shipping and its expensive effort to escort friendly tankers through Hormuz.

Either way, that seems good for Gulf producers: they will get some of their crude to market. But, coupled with rising production in the Americas and weak demand, it could mean a supply glut and lower prices—even with the war continuing.

That would be good for the world, but it could prolong the economic pain for Gulf states. In October the IMF projected that five of the six GCC members would contract this year (it revised its forecast for the UAE, from a 3.9% contraction to 0.2% growth, see chart). Only Oman, which sits outside the Strait of Hormuz, is expected to see meaningful growth.

With the war in limbo, expats have returned to the Gulf. Tourists are trickling back, too. But the region has hardly returned to its pre-war normal. Emirates, a state-owned airline in Dubai, carried 22% fewer passengers in the six months through to September than a year earlier. Hotel occupancy is 15-20 percentage points below normal in the city.

A protracted crisis will bring additional concerns. Supply chains are one. Oil may be getting out of the Gulf, but most other commodities, from fertiliser to helium, are stuck inside the strait. Nor is much going in the other direction. Lloyd’s List, a shipping journal, recorded just 227 container ships transiting through Hormuz since March (see chart), an average of less than one per day (the pre-war average was around 20).

While food, medicine and other essentials are still readily available, businesses across the region are struggling with shortages. Bars in Manama, Bahrain’s capital, are running out of beer. A property developer halted a project in Dubai for lack of the right bathroom fittings. Inflation has probably doubled in most Gulf countries this year, largely because shipping goods by road or air costs much more.

A second worry is that a long war will derail long-term investments. The UAE has hoped to make itself a hub for data centres. It has started considering plans to build such facilities underground in order to shield them from Iranian attack. But even if servers can be buried, the infrastructure that powers and cools them cannot. Expats in Doha fear lay-offs and project cancellations if the war continues into 2027. Saudi Arabia is struggling to pay contractors.

Prolonged war will force deep-pocketed Gulf firms and sovereign-wealth funds to spend more on mitigation—from defence to new pipelines and ports—leaving less money for efforts to diversify their economies. Other spending will be cut. Qatar is said to have slashed its foreign-aid budget by up to 85%, potentially a big blow to recipient countries such as Syria.

Governments will borrow to fill the gap. That is a third worry. Allianz, a German insurer, estimates that the Gulf states could run a collective cumulative deficit of $475bn from 2026 to 2030 (3-4% of GDP)—in the previous five years the region’s fiscal balance was close to even.

The pain will not be shared equally. The UAE can balance its budget even with relatively low oil prices and can use pipelines to bypass Hormuz. Having announced its departure from the OPEC cartel in April, it also plans to boost production. “Strait-locked” countries, such as Bahrain, have a higher break-even price and fewer workarounds. They may need help from their wealthier neighbours. But those neighbours will have less to give.

Gulf states find themselves in a curious position: most cannot afford an extended stand-off, yet most are urging Mr Trump to pursue one, because the alternative looks even worse. How long it lasts may depend on America’s new Congress. Some Democratic lawmakers argue that their midterm victory was fuelled by opposition to the war, and that they need to satisfy voters by cutting off funds for it. Others are nervous. “The president would love to be able to say he was on the brink of victory, only for the Democrats to yank it away from him,” says a congressional source.

If Congress does impose restrictions, the devil will be in the details. Halting funds for “offensive operations”, as some lawmakers suggest, could prevent Mr Trump from launching another big wave of air strikes. But it might not stop the blockade or the Hormuz escorts. Nor would it make the Iranians more amenable to a deal. It could just lock in the status quo.

Democrats will also be eager to investigate corruption in the Trump administration. Gulf states invested heavily in the president and his allies. Sources on Capitol Hill expect the UAE to come in for most scrutiny, because of its $500m stake in World Liberty Financial, a cryptocurrency firm founded by Mr Trump’s family and that of Steve Witkoff, his diplomatic envoy. Qatar gave Mr Trump a jet; Saudi Arabia has done deals with Jared Kushner, his son-in-law. They thought their investments had secured them a firm alliance with a Republican-dominated America. Now they are exasperated with Mr Trump and facing criticism from Democrats.

Iran’s economy is reeling from the blockade, but so are its neighbours. The Gulf states have deeper pockets, though. Many reckon they have no choice but to outlast Iran. The question is how much of their business model survives the wait.

articles.title: How the manosphere cashes in on male insecurity
articles.author: The Economist
articles.body_markdown:
Influencers are usually loth to admit they are not as rich as they seem. Andrew and Tristan Tate may have felt they had little choice. “The Tates are engaged in several businesses ‘teaching’ men how to earn money. It is in their interest to portray themselves on social media as uber-wealthy,” wrote lawyers for the pair in August, in an unsuccessful bid to persuade a Miami court that they would not abscond if granted bail. The Tate brothers have been held in detention since July as Britain seeks to extradite them to face charges for rape and sex trafficking (which they deny). The supercars and yachts that feature in their videos are rented or loaned as part of paid promotions. “In short, they are playing a role.”

Bragging about driving Bugattis and owning millions in cryptocurrency is characteristic of the “manosphere”, a milieu of hyper-masculine social-media influencers typified by the Tate brothers. By hawking supplements, online courses and especially casino games, they are shaping men’s spending across the globe. And although many of their more ostentatious displays of wealth are a mirage, the industry as a whole is roaring.

The manosphere has been around in various forms for many years, but gained new attention in 2024 as bro-ish podcasters like Joe Rogan were credited with convincing young men to vote for Donald Trump. The term is fuzzy, encompassing more mainstream self-improvement influencers as well as controversial figures like the Tates. Few are particularly political. Instead they often focus on monetising young men’s insecurity, whether about their looks, dating life or wealth.

Imagine a young man searching online for advice on how to get rich or find a girlfriend. He might begin on YouTube or TikTok, video platforms that host abundant manosphere content. A study in 2024 by researchers at Dublin City University examined its proliferation by creating “dummy” male accounts on YouTube Shorts and TikTok. All were served manosphere videos—such as ones showing them how to live an “alpha-male” lifestyle or disparaging women—within 26 minutes.

According to Fabric Media, a data provider, ten leading manosphere influencers have this year received a combined 3.4bn views across their accounts on YouTube, TikTok, Instagram and Facebook. Even that understates their reach. Many of the biggest creators pay “clippers” to cut down their videos into shorter versions and circulate them online. Clipping can be a brisk business, says Aleksa Ibrahimovic, founder of Cliptic, which provides the service. He says top influencers in manosphere-oriented categories often spend $500,000 each month paying him and his rivals to distribute their content.

The ad revenue generated by views can be substantial, even if for most manosphere influencers it falls far short of the riches on show. Additional cheques come from sponsorship deals. Clavicular, known for his “looksmaxxing” content, has flogged streetwear (YoungLA). Fresh and Fit, the “#1 men’s self-improvement podcast in the WORLD!”, has done deals with a skincare brand (Tiege Hanley) and the seller of a treatment for erectile dysfunction (BlueChew). Mitchell Jackson, a publicist for Clavicular and other edgy public figures, says he believes that just as big brands took a long time to back regular influencers, so too will they eventually advertise with risky ones. “Controversial celebrities usually actually have better business sense typically than a boring celebrity,” he says.

Where the manosphere’s stars diverge from other influencers is in their willingness to court conflict. In January a video went viral in which several prominent manosphere figures partied to a song titled “Heil Hitler”. Scandals can generate a significant boost in income for creators, notes a recent report by Equimundo and Reset Tech, two advocacy organisations.

Given such incentives, it is unsurprising that many manosphere figures have been shunted to less-regulated corners of the web. Adin Ross, a major influencer, was kicked off Twitch, a live-streaming platform, in 2023 after showing an unmoderated chat featuring slurs on screen. He said at the time that the ban was “for no reason”, though he subsequently apologised and was reinstated. Clavicular was booted from YouTube for “facilitating access to websites that violate our illegal or regulated goods or services policies”, according to the platform. Braden Peters (his real name) contends that he scrupulously followed YouTube’s terms of service. (Mr Peters was also indicted on two counts of alleged rape in November, charges he denies.)

What the influencers lose in audience, they gain in profit share. YouTube gives video-makers a 55% cut of ad dollars their channels generate and 70% of membership fees. By contrast, Kick, a streaming site that many proscribed manosphere creators have flocked to, lets influencers keep 95% of their subscription dollars. It says the programme has paid $400m to creators.

Kick stars often spend much of their streaming time playing games on Stake, an online casino with which the platform shares a parent company. Indeed, the manosphere’s profits often lead back to Stake or rivals like Rainbet and Duel. Mr Peters has streamed himself playing Stake games on Kick, which he said at the beginning of 2026 paid him more than $100,000 a month. That directs audiences to the gambling site, a loop that has allowed it to become perhaps the world’s largest online casino. In December last year Stake’s co-founder Ed Craven posted data from a third-party site calculating its customer deposits at nearly $18bn, compared with $4bn for its next-biggest competitor.

Stake—whose parent company, Easygo, is based in Australia—has built its business in large part through canny navigation of the laws surrounding online gambling. Many of its overseas affiliates operate from gambling-friendly jurisdictions like Curaçao and Cyprus. In some places it operates as a “crypto casino”, where players use digital currency to make bets.

In America its affiliate, Stake.us, uses a gap in gambling law that allows sites to operate so long as they run “sweepstakes” rather than casino games. The workaround is drawing increased scrutiny from some American states, which allege it violates laws prohibiting online gambling.

Much of Stake’s success is thanks to the influencers who direct viewers its way, Easygo’s marketing chief said in an interview last year. Kick streamers often seem to win money easily on Stake. One lawsuit claims that big stars appear to be gambling with house money rather than their own (which the company denies).

Just as looksmaxxers have led young men to stock up on hair-loss treatments, the manosphere’s ties to sites such as Stake may be helping to shift how they think about wagering cash. In one poll conducted this year, a third of Americans said they expected better returns from gambling than the stock market. The manosphere’s influence stretches far.
